# Infancy & early childhood

> *An infant grows faster than at any other time of life, on a diet that starts as a single fluid.
> The clinician's task is to fill the few nutrient gaps that milk leaves, time solids and allergens
> well and, often, gently correct a well-meant tradition.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why solids begin at about 6 months with iron-rich first foods, and how readiness signs set
  the start for an individual infant.
- Explain how early oral exposure to peanut and egg builds tolerance, and refer the high-risk infant
  for specialist-guided peanut introduction.
- Identify the three nutrient gaps of the breastfed infant (vitamin D, vitamin K and iron) and how
  each is filled.
- Interpret the evidence for breastfeeding as specific benefits with their limits, and support formula
  and mixed feeding, including safe preparation.
- Apply the division of responsibility to fussy eating and food refusal.
- Recognise the infant food-safety hazards (honey, choking hazards, added sugar and salt) and advise on
  each, and recognise the preterm, low-birth-weight or faltering infant who needs referral.
:::

## Infancy & early childhood at a glance: two drivers {#sec-overview}

Infancy and early childhood run from birth to about the pre-school years; the focus here is the
healthy term infant and young child. From about 4 to 5 years, a child eats essentially family foods
and school-age nutrition begins (see the [*Childhood & adolescence*](childhood-adolescence.qmd)
chapter). As at every life stage, the needs follow from two drivers, one inside the body and one
outside it:

| Driver | What changes at this stage |
|---|---|
| Internal drivers (inside the body) | The fastest growth of life; an immature gut, kidney and immune system; iron stores that run low at about 6 months; a developing microbiome; a brief window to accept allergens; an innate wariness of new foods |
| External levers (life and environment) | Breast milk or formula; when and how solids arrive; which foods are introduced when; food safety; the family environment the child eats in |

Most recommendations for this stage match an external lever to an internal driver, and many are
tied to age:

::: {.flow}
[Feeding timeline for the healthy term infant]{.tree-title}

1. Birth: vitamin K injection; vitamin D drops if any breast milk
2. From 4 months, if ready: iron-rich first foods, with peanut and egg
3. About 6 months: the usual start, as iron stores run low
4. By about 9 to 10 months: lumpy textures
5. About 12 months: cow's milk as main drink; honey allowed from 12 months
6. About 4 years: whole nuts and whole grapes allowed
:::

The sorter below groups common first foods by when, and in what form, each is safe.

<div data-island="food-form-sorter" data-src="/diagrams/food-form-sorter.yml"></div>

## What changes inside: iron stores and allergen tolerance {#sec-solids}

### Starting solids: timing and iron-rich first foods {#sec-starting-solids}

The question parents ask most, "when do we start?", has a physiological answer. Solids begin at
about 6 months because the iron stores present at birth are running out, so the first foods must be
iron-rich: fortified cereal, minced meat or fish, egg, legumes and tofu [@baker2010iron]. Zinc is the other nutrient most likely to fall short, and the first foods carry no added salt or sugar, because the infant kidney is immature and taste preferences are being set [@whoComplementaryFeeding2023].

The infant's readiness, not the calendar, sets the start for each child. A ready infant shows four
signs, usually near 6 months and not before 4 months:

- sits with support;
- has steady head control;
- has lost the **tongue-thrust reflex**, which pushes food out of the mouth;
- reaches for food.

The 4-month floor reconciles two guideline positions. WHO holds to "about 6 months", whereas allergy
and gastroenterology societies argue for starting solids, including allergens, between 4 and 6
months [@whoComplementaryFeeding2023; @fewtrell2024multisociety]. The two apply at different levels:
"about 6 months" is the population default, and 4 months is the floor for an individual infant who
is ready. Singapore's guidelines take the same position (see [The Singapore picture](#sec-singapore)).

Cow's milk waits until about 12 months as the main drink, for the same iron reason. It is iron-poor
and, in infancy, causes occult (hidden) blood loss from the gut, a direct route to iron deficiency
[@ziegler1990cowmilk; @ziegler2011review]. Small amounts of yoghurt or cheese are fine as
**complementary foods** (solids given alongside milk) from 6 months, so the line falls between cow's milk as the main drink and dairy
as a food.

The aim is to prevent iron deficiency before it starts. Iron deficiency in the brain-growth
window between 6 and 24 months can leave neurocognitive effects that persist into adulthood despite
later iron, which is the strongest argument for getting the first foods right [@lukowski2010iron].

Textures also have to progress. Introducing lumps later than about 9 to 10 months is linked to more
feeding difficulty years later, so food moves from purée to mashed to soft finger foods on schedule,
and parents learn to tell normal, protective gagging from true choking [@coulthard2009texture].

### Early allergen introduction: peanut and egg {#sec-allergens}

For years the advice was to delay peanut and egg "to be safe". Trials have since reversed that
advice, and the mechanism explains why. Two immune outcomes are possible when an infant first meets
a food. **Sensitisation** primes the immune system to react to it; **tolerance** is acceptance, so
eating the food causes no reaction. The **dual-allergen hypothesis** holds that the route of first
exposure decides which occurs: inflamed, eczematous skin sensitises, whereas meeting the food by
mouth first builds tolerance [@lack2008dual]. Early oral introduction therefore protects.

The trial evidence agrees. The LEAP trial gave high-risk infants (those with severe eczema or egg
allergy) peanut early and cut peanut allergy by around 80% [@dutoit2015leap]. The EAT trial pointed
the same way, with adherence the practical limit, and a meta-analysis confirmed the effect for peanut
and egg [@perkin2016eat; @ierodiakonou2016].

In practice, smooth peanut butter and well-cooked egg are introduced once solids begin. One caution
applies: LEAP studied only these high-risk infants, so its 80% figure does not transfer to every
infant (the high-risk infant is referred; see [Recognising trouble, and when to
refer](#sec-hazards)).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: iron stores run low at about 6 months. Why does that keep cow's milk from being the main drink until about 12 months?
As the main drink, cow's milk is iron-poor and causes occult blood loss from the infant gut, a direct
route to iron deficiency just as the iron stores present at birth run out. Iron deficiency between 6
and 24 months can leave lasting neurocognitive effects. Small amounts of yoghurt or cheese are still
fine as complementary foods, so the rule is about cow's milk as the main drink, not dairy as a food.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: for years parents were told to delay peanut and egg. Why does early introduction protect instead?
In the dual-allergen hypothesis, an infant becomes sensitised to a food through inflamed, eczematous
skin but develops tolerance by meeting it by mouth first, so early oral introduction builds
tolerance. LEAP cut peanut allergy by around 80%, and a meta-analysis confirmed the effect for peanut
and egg. LEAP's 80% figure comes from high-risk infants (those with severe eczema or egg allergy), so
it does not transfer to every infant.
:::

## What changes outside: breast milk, formula and responsive feeding {#sec-milk}

### Breast milk: composition, evidence and gaps {#sec-breast-milk}

Breast milk changes in composition, both as it matures after birth and within each feed. It matures from
**colostrum**, the low-volume, antibody-dense milk of the first days, to mature milk. Colostrum is
sometimes called a "first vaccine", and its small volume is often mistaken for "not enough milk
yet". Within a single feed, the watery **foremilk** gives way to the fat-rich **hindmilk**
[@ballard2013milk].

Two components of breast milk do work that no formula fully copies. **Secretory IgA**, an antibody,
coats the infant's gut and blocks pathogens while the infant's own immunity matures. Human milk
oligosaccharides (HMOs), sugars the infant cannot digest (see [*The
gut microbiome*](gut-microbiome.qmd#sec-development) chapter), selectively feed *Bifidobacterium*.
Feeding *Bifidobacterium* seeds the infant microbiome and, through short-chain fatty acids, supports
the gut barrier [@ballard2013milk; @dinleyici2023hmo].

The slogan "breast is best" needs reading against the evidence. The cleanest data come from
PROBIT, a large cluster-randomised trial of breastfeeding support, which found real reductions in
gastrointestinal infection and eczema but no reduction in respiratory infection
[@kramer2001probit]. Its cognitive benefit at 6.5 years was modest and mostly verbal
[@kramer2008cognition], and by 16 years only a much smaller verbal effect remained [@yang2018probit]. In observational studies the association with IQ is small, and
it shrinks after adjustment for the mother's own IQ [@horta2015iq].

Breastfeeding is also associated with modestly lower later obesity, about 15% lower odds in the
least-biased studies, but this is an association, not proof of cause [@horta2023obesity].
Counselling therefore states the specific benefits without overselling them.

Breast milk leaves three nutrient gaps, and each has a standard remedy (the nutrient science is in
the [*Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter):

| Nutrient | The gap | How it is filled |
|---|---|---|
| Vitamin D | Breast milk is low in vitamin D | 400 IU/day from birth for every breastfed or partially breastfed infant [@meek2022breastfeeding] |
| Vitamin K | Breast milk is low in vitamin K | A single injection at birth |
| Iron | The stores present at birth last about 6 months, then deplete | Iron-rich first foods from about 6 months |

Vitamin D is the one routine daily infant supplement. **Vitamin K deficiency bleeding** is bleeding
in newborns and young infants caused by too little vitamin K. Because breast milk is low in
vitamin K, breastfed infants are the most prone to it, and the single injection at birth prevents
it [@hand2022vitk]. The depletion of iron stores at about 6 months sets the timing of solids (see
[Starting solids](#sec-starting-solids)).

The recommendation built on the evidence above and these gaps is **exclusive breastfeeding**
(breast milk only, with no other food or drink apart from vitamin drops or medicines) for about 6
months. After that come complementary foods, with continued
breastfeeding into the second year, supported by the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative
[@whoBreastfeeding]. The recommendation is applied with the iron and allergen caveats above
[@kramer2012cochrane].

### Formula and mixed feeding {#sec-formula}

Most infants receive some formula, and the counselling posture is support, not shame. Modern infant
formula is safe and nutritionally adequate, so the clinician's contribution is safe preparation.
Powdered formula is not sterile: it is made up with water at 70 °C or above to kill *Cronobacter* (a
bacterium that can contaminate the powder), then cooled, and any made-up feed is discarded after 2
hours [@faoWhoPif2007].

**Mixed feeding**, giving both breast milk and formula, is the norm, not a failure. In Singapore only
about 3% of infants are exclusively breastfed at 6 months, while most still receive some breast
milk, so breast milk plus formula is the usual pattern [@sgBreastfeeding2024]. When you see a mother
who is mixed feeding, support the pattern practically; the vitamin D dose still applies to any
partially breastfed infant.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Feeding well in Singapore: cost and shared caregiving
Premium formulas and toddler milks add cost, not nutrition: every infant formula sold in Singapore
meets the same standard, yet prices have more than doubled. After 12 months, plain full-fat cow's
milk does the job, so toddler (or "growing-up") milks are unnecessary and often sugar-sweetened
[@cccsFormula2017; @fuchs2023toddlermilk]. Feeding here is also a family activity, often led by
grandparents and confinement caregivers (carers who look after mother and baby during the
traditional period of rest after birth). They carry beliefs worth gently addressing, such as that
fruit can stand in for vegetables or that a child should always finish the plate, so counsel the
whole household that feeds the child [@tanGrandparents2019].
:::

### Responsive feeding and fussy eating {#sec-responsive-feeding}

How a child is fed matters as much as what. **Responsive feeding** follows the child's hunger and
fullness cues. The organising idea for feeding a young child is the **division of
responsibility**: the parent decides what, when and where, and the child decides whether and how
much [@satterDoR].

Two findings explain why the division works. First, toddlers pass through a phase of **food
neophobia**, refusing new foods on sight. The phase is usually transient (most fussy eating resolves
within a couple of years) and yields to repeated, low-pressure offering, on the order of 8 to 15
tries [@spill2019exposure; @mascola2010picky]. Second, pressure backfires: "finish your plate" is
associated with more fussiness, not less. A fussy child also draws more pressure from parents, so
the association runs both ways [@jansen2017pressure].

**Baby-led weaning**, in which the infant feeds itself instead of being spoon-fed, is a reasonable
parent choice when an iron-rich food is offered at each meal; it is no better and no worse than
spoon-feeding on iron [@daniels2018bliss]. Choking depends on food form, not on the feeding method:
about a third of infants choke at least once between 6 and 8 months, at a similar rate whichever
way they are fed [@fangupo2016choking].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a healthy term breastfed baby is given vitamin D drops from birth, but no iron drops. Why the difference?
Breast milk is low in vitamin D from the start, so every breastfed or partially breastfed infant
needs 400 IU/day from birth. Iron is different: a term infant's stores present at birth last about
6 months, so the iron gap opens later and is filled by iron-rich first foods, not drops. The same
depletion of iron stores at about 6 months sets the timing of solids.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: only about 3% of Singapore infants are exclusively breastfed at 6 months. What follows for a mother who is mixed feeding?
Mixed feeding is the usual pattern, not a failure, so she gets practical support without shame.
Formula is safe and adequate, so the useful advice is safe preparation: water at 70 °C or above to
kill *Cronobacter*, cooling, and discarding any made-up feed after 2 hours. Because her baby still
receives some breast milk, the 400 IU/day vitamin D dose still applies.
:::

## Recognising trouble, and when to refer {#sec-hazards}

Three rules prevent avoidable harm in the first years:

- No honey before 12 months. The immature gut lets *Clostridium botulinum* spores from honey colonise
  and make toxin, causing **infant botulism** [@harris2024botulism].
- No choking hazards (high-risk food shapes) before about 4 years: no whole nuts, whole grapes, hard
  raw vegetables or chunks of hot dog. Grapes are quartered lengthwise and food is cut small
  [@aap2010choking].
- No added sugar or salt, no sugary drinks, and no fruit juice before 12 months (and little juice
  after); early sweetness sets a lasting preference [@heyman2017juice;
  @whoComplementaryFeeding2023].

A few infants need more than the default advice for the healthy term infant, and are referred.
Preterm and low-birth-weight infants are the first case. Their iron stores deplete earlier and
their solids are timed by **corrected age** (age counted from the due date), so their feeding is
individualised.

The infant at high risk of allergy (severe eczema or egg allergy) is the second; for this infant,
peanut introduction is specialist-guided instead of improvised. The third is the infant with
faltering growth (faltering growth is among the refer triggers in the
[*Childhood & adolescence*](childhood-adolescence.qmd) chapter). The referral cues are summarised
below:

| Sign | Action |
|---|---|
| Preterm or low birth weight | Individualise feeding, with solids timed by corrected age; refer |
| High risk of allergy (severe eczema or egg allergy) | Refer for specialist-guided peanut introduction |
| Faltering growth | Refer |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: whole peanuts are kept from children until about 4 years, yet smooth peanut butter is encouraged from the start of solids. Why?
Choking depends on food form, not on the food itself or the feeding method. A whole nut is a choking
shape, so peanut is offered as smooth peanut butter instead, and early oral peanut builds tolerance.
The same logic makes a grape quartered lengthwise safe where a whole grape is not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: iron-rich solids at about 6 months and early peanut are the defaults. Why are a preterm infant and an infant with severe eczema referred?
The defaults are set for the healthy term infant. A preterm or low-birth-weight infant's iron stores
deplete earlier, and solids are timed by corrected age (age counted from the due date), so feeding is
individualised. An infant with severe eczema is at high risk of allergy (the group LEAP studied:
severe eczema or egg allergy), and for this infant peanut introduction is specialist-guided instead
of improvised.
:::

## Is "breast is best" the whole story? {#sec-close}

Breast milk is a strong start, not a complete one. It leaves three specific gaps (vitamin D,
vitamin K and iron), and formula and mixed feeding are safe alternatives. Much of what protects an
infant lies beyond the milk itself:

- iron-rich first foods at about 6 months, because the iron stores present at birth run out;
- early peanut and egg, because oral exposure builds tolerance;
- the honey, cow's-milk and choking rules, because each prevents a specific, avoidable harm;
- responsive feeding, because pressure to eat backfires.

A large part of the clinician's work, in Singapore especially (see
[The Singapore picture](#sec-singapore)), is gently retiring a well-meant tradition. Another part is
recognising the few infants (preterm, high allergy risk, faltering growth) who need more than the
default advice, and referring them.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**Singapore has its own feeding guidelines for the first 2 years.** The national consensus
guidelines are built around variety, autonomy, an unhurried screen-free setting and sensible timing.
Their practical advice includes five points [@smjFeeding2023]:

- vegetables as the first complementary food, to build acceptance of vegetables (offered alongside the iron-rich first foods of [Starting solids](#sec-starting-solids));
- responsive feeding from birth;
- complementary foods at 4 to 6 months;
- specialist-guided early peanut for high-risk infants;
- cow's milk as a drink only after 12 months.

**Breastfeeding starts well but rarely stays exclusive.** Nearly every mother starts breastfeeding,
but exclusive breastfeeding falls to about 3% by 6 months, so the sensible posture is realistic
support plus non-judgemental formula guidance [@sgBreastfeeding2024]. Formula marketing to the
under-ones is restricted by a local ethics code [@sifecsCode].

**First foods are usually rice-based.** Congee is a fine first food if it is made iron-rich with
minced meat, egg and soft greens, not served as plain rice-water [@tohFeeding2016].

**Caregiving is shared.** Counselling on the common feeding patterns, such as pushing a child to
finish, feeding in front of screens and prolonged night bottles, has to reach grandparents and
helpers as well as parents [@quahFeeding2025].

**Sunshine does not replace the vitamin D drops.** The vitamin D dose matters here precisely because
infant sun exposure is, rightly, kept low.

## Practise: a new-parent feeding clinic {#sec-case}

Baby Aidan, a thriving breastfed 5-month-old, comes to a routine visit with his mother. She brings
worries about solids, allergens, honey, cow's milk and formula from the internet, the family and a
neighbour. Work through the visit: sort the evidence from the
tradition, correct it kindly, and know when to refer. Your choices branch the case.
